evidence.topic: How mine salting made a poor mine seem valuable; general demonstration, not a named invented event

facts.quote: Luxurious rewards awaited the bunco artist who could make gold seem to appear in a hole where no gold actually existed, or the con man who could produce, for suspicious examining engineers, specimens of silver that assayed higher (as the gulled buyer discovered too late) than the ore body from which they supposedly came.

Nor was it necessary to sprinkle the salt, as the fraudulent additive was called, throughout the exposed ore—that would have been too expensive—but only in those samples, taken here and there, from which the valuation of the mine was calculated.
a property on Signal hill, Cripple creek, within less than a mile from the town, was salted by using chloride of gold in a shotgun, shooting it into the breasts of the drifts and bottom of the shaft.
facts.note: Historical source reports gold chloride, not gold nuggets. Existing gold_shotgun renders nuggets. Do not depict this exact chemical method as nuggets; prefer a general sample-contamination explanation unless matching geometry exists.

facts.quote: The basis of an engineer's detection of salting is on the principle of inconsistency of results.
facts.note: No evidence that every flattened flake proves shotgun fraud. No invented rich buyer, expert dialogue, explosion or real vein ending.
